slides.title: Open Rack Architecture and the Open Ecosystem
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Open Rack. Developed through the Open Compute Project, Open Rack is an open platform for data center racks, power distribution, and equipment interfaces. Its shared designs help organizations build efficient, scalable computing infrastructure.

We'll begin with Open Rack's origins and the ideas behind it, then explore its key features and the power and cooling systems that support today's demanding workloads.

slides.title: Your Route Through the Seven Modules
slides.transcript: The seven modules follow one engineering review, from defining the workload to deciding whether a complete rack is ready. You'll examine interfaces, calculate usable power, compare architectures, and identify missing evidence. Expert walkthroughs and technical animations bring these ideas to life. The core path is designed for about two hours and twenty-five minutes. Specialist Academy courses offer optional deeper study.

slides.title: Start with the Workload, Then Define the Rack
slides.transcript:
A rack choice starts with what the deployment must do. Specify the equipment population and its expected operating envelope, rather than choosing a frame and hoping the workload fits. Sustained demand, short excursions, cooling conditions and acceptable behavior during a fault can lead to different designs even at the same advertised rack power.

Next, identify the constraints that equipment creates. Weight and center of gravity affect support and handling. Cable and hose routes affect installation and service. Heat that isn't captured by liquid still needs an air path. A maintenance strategy may require access that an otherwise compatible layout obstructs.

Turn these needs into a requirements sheet with measurable conditions and an owner for every unresolved item. For example, a cooling requirement should identify the permitted operating conditions and the interface where they're guaranteed, not just say liquid cooled. Keep the initial design envelope explicit. Later modules will use it to distinguish a product that looks suitable from a deployment with enough evidence to proceed.

slides.title: From ORv1 to ORv3 and ORW
slides.transcript:
Open Rack evolved as operators sought shared interfaces and more flexible infrastructure. The useful history is the sequence of constraints, not a list of dates. A shared mechanical arrangement helps equipment integrate. Rack-level power distribution changes where conversion and distribution hardware sit. Increasing density makes electrical, thermal and service boundaries more demanding.

Open Rack version three, or ORv3, is our main starting point. High-power rack implementations extend the power architecture for heavier loads. Open Rack Wide, or ORW, expands the mechanical envelope to support different equipment packaging and integration needs. These are related developments, not interchangeable names for one rack with ever-larger ratings.

The animation builds this progression around the constraint each step addresses. Notice that changing the frame doesn't automatically validate its electrical system, and adding power doesn't establish cooling capacity. We will use version and implementation names precisely throughout the course. When a claim includes dimensions, mass or power, the next question is which document, configuration and revision make that claim true.

slides.video_transcript: Welcome to this OCP Academy course on Open Rack and ORv3. In this first lesson, we'll look at how the Open Compute Project began and how it shaped the Open Rack standard that so many modern data centers rely on today. The Open Compute Project, or OCP, was founded in 2011 by Facebook, now Meta, together with Intel and Rackspace. Their goal was to share open source hardware designs that could make data centers more efficient, scalable, and sustainable. The origins of Open Rack go back to Facebook's need to scale its infrastructure efficiently. Traditional data center designs were full of inefficiencies that added cost and complexity. The first Open Rack standard, called ORv1, launched in 2012 to 2013. Its centralized power distribution with a 12v DC power shelf and busbars. This reduced the number of server power cables and made racks easier to service. After ORv1, the community developed ORv2. It improved power and rack designs, but was mainly focused on hyperscale data centers, using 21 -inch servers and direct current power. This made it less common for wider enterprise use, which followed the traditional American Electronic Industries Alliance, EIA, standardized 19 -inch rack. By 2016, the community knew that new challenges like artificial intelligence and high -performance computing would require even higher power densities and better cooling. So development of ORv3 began. From 2016 to 2018, companies like Meta, Google, and Microsoft worked together to identify the need for higher power density, better cooling solutions, and more flexibility for both hyperscale and enterprise data centers. By 2019 and 2020, contributors like Advanced Energy were developing ORv3 power shelves that used a 48v DC architecture. This increased efficiency and supported more power -hungry workloads. In 2021, the OCP Global Summit showcased ORv3's readiness for broader adoption. Power shelves demonstrated 97 .5 % efficiency and up to 36kW in a 2OU form factor. By 2022, ORv3 was ready for full -scale deployment. ORv3 was designed to be flexible. It supports both 21 -inch open -compute equipment and older, standard 19 -inch equipment. It also includes features like liquid cooling manifolds and blindmate power connections to make installation easier. By 2024, adoption of ORv3 had grown significantly. Companies like Cheval, Eaton, Flex, Rittal, and Sanmina have their racks in the OCP marketplace based on the ORv3 specification. You'll even find racks from wooden data centers made from low -embedded carbon materials. In 2025, companies like Meta and NVIDIA contributed advanced designs such as the Catalina, an MGX AI rack, and Compute Shelf, which can handle up to 140kW per rack for powerful AI workloads. ORv3 has changed the data center industry by improving power efficiency, boosting cooling capabilities, and creating a more flexible open ecosystem. Today, the OCP continues to drive collaboration and standard specifications. Its open -source hardware approach helps data centers around the world scale for the future while staying efficient and sustainable with ever -increasing demands of higher performance computing to power artificial intelligence that, in turn, will boost the human intelligence behind every industry.

slides.title: The Rack as a System of Interfaces
slides.transcript:
Think of the rack as a system of interfaces. The mechanical interface locates and supports equipment, but also reserves clearance for connections and removal. Electrical interfaces define how power reaches that equipment and what behavior is permitted during connection, operation and faults. Thermal interfaces define the conditions under which heat can leave.

Management adds another boundary: what is measured, which controller can request a change, and who owns the response. Service ties the interfaces together. A replaceable item isn't practically serviceable if removing it strains an energized connection or blocks an adjacent cooling circuit.

The figure reveals each boundary separately, then brings them together. This is a conceptual map, not a wiring drawing. Use it to ask a precise question at each handoff: what does one side provide, what does the other side require, and what evidence shows agreement? A shared rack family can reduce integration work, but it doesn't eliminate these questions. The resulting interface review is the organizing tool we'll carry through the remaining modules.

slides.title: Base Specifications, Implementations and IT Gear
slides.transcript:
Not every document in a rack project has the same authority. The base specification establishes shared interfaces within its scope. An implementation specification describes a particular design, including choices that the base leaves open. A design guide helps equipment authors apply those interfaces, but its guidance isn't automatically a new mandatory requirement.

The ORv3 IT Gear Design Guide makes this distinction explicitly: firm requirements reside in the base specification. Read the relevant requirement and its applicability before treating advice as a pass or fail criterion. Likewise, don't transfer a dimension or payload from an implementation document to the entire Open Rack family.

During a review, record the exact document, revision and supporting page. Then connect the claim to the supplied product and its configuration. A supplier can reasonably implement an allowed option without matching another operator's design. The task is to establish which interfaces must agree, which choices are permitted, and whether the selected equipment is qualified together. This prevents both unnecessary rejection and unsupported compatibility claims.

slides.title: Follow Energy In and Heat Out
slides.transcript:
Follow the energy path into the rack, then follow the heat out. Power passes through conversion and distribution stages before reaching the workload. Each stage has limits, losses, protection behavior and an operating envelope. A rating at one stage doesn't establish what reaches the equipment after every other constraint is applied.

For cooling, identify both the liquid path and the residual air path. The rack may connect to a coolant distribution unit, or CDU, with a separate facility-side loop. Don't assume those fluids, pressures or temperatures are interchangeable. A thermal boundary needs a defined condition and a responsible party on each side.

This first map doesn't require detailed electrical or hydraulic calculations. It requires the boundaries to be visible. Mark where the facility commitment ends, where the rack integrator's responsibility begins, and what the equipment supplier assumes. If two parties each assume the other provides the same function, the diagram has exposed a real integration risk. Resolve that gap before turning individual component ratings into a system claim.

slides.title: One Rack Family, Different Implementations
slides.transcript:
Two racks can share an interface family and still differ in consequential ways. External dimensions, equipment supports, power-shelf arrangements, cooling integration and handling features may depend on the implementation. A compatible connection in one location doesn't make every part of the two systems interchangeable.

High-power designs may separate power equipment from the IT rack or use different distribution arrangements. A wider rack can change equipment packaging, but it also changes the site route and service envelope. These choices have to be reviewed as a configuration, not assembled from the most attractive rating in each document.

For a useful comparison, hold the deployment requirements constant. Ask each supplier to identify the product revision, supported equipment population, operating conditions and evidence for those conditions. Record deliberate differences rather than hiding them beneath a common ORv3 label. A family name helps you find the right starting documents. It cannot replace the configuration-specific review needed to accept a rack into service.

slides.title: Modularity Becomes an Operational Benefit
slides.transcript:
Modularity matters when it changes an operational decision. If equipment can evolve without replacing the supporting infrastructure, an operator may extend useful life or choose between qualified suppliers. Shared interfaces also make repair and staged upgrades easier to plan.

These benefits are conditional. A replacement part must meet the relevant mechanical, electrical, thermal and management requirements. A later revision can change behavior even when the connector still fits. Reuse therefore needs condition assessment and documented compatibility, not just the absence of visible damage.

Consider replacing one equipment generation while retaining the rack and power distribution. Mechanical fit is only the first check. The new equipment may draw a different peak current, reject heat differently or need additional telemetry. The retained infrastructure must support the new envelope, including the agreed fault case. Treat modularity as a way to create options with evidence. It is not permission to mix unqualified assemblies, and it doesn't remove the need to control revisions throughout the deployment's life.

slides.title: Read the Evidence Before the Marketing
slides.transcript:
A requirement, a product claim and a roadmap answer different questions. A requirement states what a scoped design must meet. A test report describes observed behavior under particular conditions. A roadmap describes intended future work. None should silently substitute for another.

The same discipline applies to recognition. Use the precise status recorded for the named product in the OCP Marketplace or contribution record. Don't turn recognition into a blanket certification of every possible rack configuration or supplier combination. Check what was actually reviewed and what remains the integrator's responsibility.

Summit material is especially useful for understanding emerging constraints and engineering approaches. We'll use twenty twenty-six examples, but distinguish published contributions from reference designs, prototypes and future plans. When a result matters to acceptance, ask for the current design revision, test configuration, boundary conditions and outstanding limitations. That information makes the evidence actionable. A compelling diagram or a large headline rating alone doesn't establish readiness for your deployment.

slides.title: Design Review Case: Define the Deployment Envelope
slides.transcript:
Our running case is a dense accelerator deployment with liquid cooling, constrained site access and a requirement to grow. It is a teaching scenario, not a specification for a real installation. The team has a rack proposal and several attractive component ratings, but hasn't yet demonstrated that the complete configuration meets its operating envelope.

Start an evidence record with five headings: mechanical and payload, power, thermal, site route, and service and control. For each, record the requirement, proposed solution, supporting evidence and unresolved issue. An unresolved issue needs an owner and a closure condition, not a vague assurance that it will be handled later.

At each stage we'll choose go, conditional go or hold. Conditional go means a bounded next activity is permitted with explicit restrictions; it doesn't mean commissioning is approved. Hold means a missing or conflicting item blocks the requested activity. Pause and identify one question you'd ask under each heading. We'll refine those questions as the interfaces and failure cases become concrete.

slides.title: Read the Frame from Its Datums
slides.transcript:
Mechanical compatibility depends on reference geometry, not just overall width. A datum is the reference used to locate a feature. When two drawings use different references, apparently similar dimensions can describe different positions. Read the datum, orientation and tolerance before comparing numbers.

The ORv3 base specification allows alternative frame geometries and leaves external dimensions to the rack developer. The shared interfaces still have to agree. Identify the selected option and use its drawing consistently. Don't combine one option's support geometry with another option's connection location.

A keep-out is reserved space, not unused space available for an extra bracket. It can protect connector travel, tubing movement, tools or a replacement path. Check the equipment in its installed and service positions, including accumulated tolerances and allowable deflection. A tray can rest on its supports while its rear interfaces are outside their permitted alignment. Treat the source drawing as the controlling geometry; the simplified course figure is a reading aid, not a fabrication drawing.

slides.video_transcript: Welcome to this detailed look inside the ORv3 frame. In this lesson, we'll identify the key physical specifications of Open Rack version 3, including its updated dimensions, the busbar system, and the power shelf that makes it so efficient for modern data centers. The ORv3 rack is the result of years of development work and collaboration between rack and component vendors, as well as the hyperscalers and wider OCP community. Over the last three years, this design has evolved to address the changing needs of high density, scalable data centers. Let's start at the front of the rack. One of the first physical features you'll notice is the new modular cable manager. This modular piece can be unscrewed and removed to allow for customized cable management across the entire aisle. Modular cable management gives operators the flexibility to organize cables neatly and adjust layouts as needs change, which helps with airflow and maintenance in large -scale deployments. Inside the rack frame, ORv3 can now accommodate both OU and RU shelves from top to bottom. In ORv2, there was only Open U positioning, but now standard rack units are supported too. This expanded shelf support means that operators can install more equipment with standard sizing, making the rack more versatile for different IT gear. Another key update is that these shelves are designed to be tool -less, saving time during installation. Now let's move to the back of the rack. One of the biggest improvements here is the upgraded busbar power system. In the previous version, ORv2 racks used a 12v busbar, but ORv3 has stepped up to a 48v system. This upgrade to 48v delivers higher power efficiency and greater capacity, which is crucial for AI and HPC workloads that require denser power distribution. The busbar is fully integrated into the rack frame, with easy access for connecting power shelves and IT gear. It's one of the core features that sets Open Rack apart from traditional designs. In addition to the busbar, ORv3 racks include features that future -proof the frame for advanced cooling. The frame has dedicated spaces to support cold -arm cooling manifolds when liquid cooling becomes more widely adopted. This means that as AI servers push power rack requirements higher, operators can switch from air cooling to liquid cooling without replacing the entire rack structure. Structurally, the ORv3 frame is built to handle heavy loads. Each rack can now dynamically support up to 1400kg, which has been tested and approved. This is an increase in strength and stability compared to previous designs. Having a higher load capacity means more equipment can be installed without compromising stability or airflow. This is especially important for data centers that are constantly upgrading or retrofitting equipment. All these features combined make the ORv3 rack more flexible, powerful, and ready for the demands of next -generation workloads. From its improved cable management to the upgraded busbar and shelf system, every design choice supports efficiency and scalability.

slides.title: OpenU and RU Are Different Grids
slides.transcript:
Open U and the conventional rack unit are different vertical grids. The ORv3 base specification describes forty-eight millimeter Open U spacing and forty-four point four-five millimeter rack-unit spacing. The difference accumulates across a stack, so these labels aren't interchangeable ways to count height.

The selected rack features, supports and equipment mounting arrangement determine what can be installed. An adapter can address a defined mechanical interface, but it doesn't automatically establish the power connector location, service access or cooling arrangement. Review those separately.

For a mixed-equipment proposal, mark the grid used by each item and the reference used to locate its connections. Check both the occupied envelope and the required installation movement. Avoid inferring compatibility from the number printed next to U on a product sheet. The practical outcome is a stack arrangement that is supported and aligned at every required interface, rather than a height total that happens to fit inside the frame.

slides.video_transcript: In high -performance and AI -optimized data centers, thermal management is no longer just a matter of airflow. It's a fundamental design priority. The ORv3 specification integrates both air and liquid cooling support directly into the rack infrastructure, enabling flexibility across deployment types and workloads. Let's start with air cooling. ORv3 racks maintain compatibility with traditional air -cooled systems by supporting consistent front -to -rear airflow through the rack and chassis. This ensures that even legacy or mixed environment deployments remain viable, allowing a gradual transition to advanced cooling without a full infrastructure overhaul. However, as compute densities rise, especially in AI, HPC, and GPU -intensive environments, air alone isn't sufficient. That's where liquid cooling enters the frame. ORv3 introduces native support for Direct Liquid Cooling, or DLC, through a robust, blindmate manifold interface. This manifold sits at the back of the rack and serves as a shared thermal exchange interface for all DLC -compatible IT gear. A key feature is the rear blindmate connection. Each DLC -compatible sled or chassis is fitted with a cold plate interface that connects seamlessly to the manifold without requiring tools or human intervention. This allows for hot swapping of gear even in liquid -cooled environments, reducing service downtime and risk of leaks. The manifold itself is engineered for high flow capacity and thermal efficiency. It typically supports 12mm quick disconnect couplings, but the spec allows flexibility in connector design provided they meet OCP -compliant standards. It's also modular, enabling single or multi -loop configurations to accommodate variable thermal loads within the same rack. ORv3 also accommodates coolant distribution units, or CDUs, located externally or internally, depending on deployment. These CDUs circulate and manage coolant through the rack loop, often interfacing with facility -side cooling systems such as cooling towers or heat exchangers. Another ORv3 advantage is sustainability through higher thermal set points. By allowing safe operation at higher inlet temperatures, often in the 27°C to 32°C range, ORv3 racks reduce the energy needed for chilling, aligning with ASHRAE A1 standards and enabling broader use of free cooling or warm water cooling loops. Finally, air flow and liquid cooling are not mutually exclusive. Many ORv3 deployments adopt hybrid cooling strategies, combining air -cooled IT gear with liquid -cooled accelerators or GPUs in the same rack. The rack design supports this mixed configuration through flexible mounting and airflow containment options. Together, these cooling innovations make ORv3 a highly adaptable platform for future -ready thermal management. Whether you're operating traditional servers or AI clusters pushing 100 kW per rack,

A clean empty-frame layout can become unserviceable when populated. Cables and hoses occupy volume, need support and move during installation or replacement. Their permitted routing and bend conditions belong in the configuration review, not in an improvised field arrangement.

Reserve the tool and hand access required by the approved service method. Don't route a new bundle through an envelope needed to remove another item.

Review the densest permitted configuration and the service movement, not only the final resting position. Check that strain isn't transferred into a coupling or electrical connection when adjacent equipment moves. Then identify who owns changes after deployment. slides.video_transcript: Let's talk about payload compatibility. The flexibility of the ORv3 rack to support different types of IT equipment. This is a critical factor in any modern deployment, and ORv3 delivers on it. The heart of ORv3's flexibility lies in its ability to accommodate both OCP native gear and traditional EIA standard equipment. That means organizations can deploy 21 -inch wide OCP gear while still supporting legacy 19 -inch servers, switches, and other hardware. This dual compatibility is more than a convenience. It enables smoother transitions between old and new infrastructure. Operators can adopt open hardware standards gradually without needing to forklift their existing inventory. Let's start with OCP native gear. These systems are designed specifically for ORv3's 21 -inch internal bay. The added width allows for more efficient component layouts, higher airflow, and better cable routing, all within a standard 600 -millimeter rack footprint. On the flip side, ORv3 is also engineered to mount 19 -inch EIA equipment using standardized adapters. These adapter brackets, or conversion trays, allow legacy hardware to fit securely inside the wider frame, preserving alignment with airflow and mounting holes. Mounting flexibility extends to both full -width and half -width sleds. In a typical ORv3 deployment, you'll find combinations of full -width compute nodes, half -width storage sleds, or high -density AI accelerators, all within the same rack. The rack's internal rail system is designed to support these varied payload types without modification. That's especially valuable for hyperscale and enterprise teams experimenting with different IT loads or phasing in new workloads like AI inference or HPC clusters. Another benefit? Tool -less mounting. Like other aspects of ORv3, payload installation is designed to be quick and serviceable. Whether it's an OCP sled or EIA gear with brackets, IT teams can install and remove equipment without specialized tools. This hybrid -ready approach makes ORv3 a future -proof choice. As more operators adopt open hardware designs, they won't need to discard their existing EIA hardware. ORv3 provides a seamless bridge between the two ecosystems. In short, ORv3 doesn't force a choice. It welcomes innovation while respecting existing infrastructure. That adaptability is part of what makes it so widely adopted. It's open, it's efficient, and it's built for the real -world needs of today's data centers.

slides.video_transcript: When it comes to deploying ORv3 in the real world, two major players, Meta and Google, have each taken unique approaches, reflecting their scale, data center infrastructure, and evolving workload demands. These exercise different options in the ORv3 -based specification. Let's start with Meta. Meta's implementation of ORv3 builds on the standard specifications, option one with key adaptations for high performance computing. Their rack design emphasizes high availability and mechanical consistency using standardized 21 -inch IT gear form factors. It can support 44 OU total or 47 RU total units in terms of its height for payloads. It enables streamlined airflow and simplified servicing across global facilities. Power is delivered via 48V busbars, and the design accommodates high power workloads with modularity for future growth. Meta's ORv3 racks also include extended monitoring capabilities and predictable front -to -back airflow profiles, helping their infrastructure support rapid scalability while managing thermal loads efficiently. An update to Meta's frame specification with also planned and later came with high power rack versions and Meta's Catalina project and OCP contribution. On the other hand, Google's implementation offers depth options of both 32 and 48 inches. It has an OCP compliant feature set. It's capable of integrating industry standard equipment designed for EIA 19 -inch racks as well as custom payloads that are up to 24 inches wide and even greater than 36 inches deep. Furthermore, it has a load rating of 3 ,000 pounds which is on par with ORv3 specification of approximately 1 ,400 kilograms. The Google ORv3 implementation provides rear accessible flexible cable management as well as the ability to integrate both 48 volt DC power distribution as well as AC PDUs. Finally, there are provisions for rear and front accessories as well as the option for rack level EMI containment. What unites both companies is their commitment to open standards and the scalability that ORv3 provides, whether the goal is performance, sustainability, or deployment speed. ORv3 allows organizations to standardize their mechanical and electrical infrastructure, adapt to liquid cooling, and support both AI and cloud native workloads. Their contributions are also reflected in the spec documents that help evolve the ORv3 standard. Meta, Google, and others continue to iterate on ORv3 through collaborative development and transparent publishing. From hyperscale data centers to AI ready deployments, ORv3 is already powering the backbone of modern compute.

slides.title: Build a Compatibility and Evidence Matrix
slides.transcript:
An evidence matrix makes the logic behind a deployment decision visible. Start with a requirement, identify the configured interface that must satisfy it, and attach a record that actually supports the claim. Then state the review result and any remaining gap.

The animation follows a product claim through the governing document, the proposed configuration and qualification evidence. Notice the distinction between documented and demonstrated. A drawing can specify an intended relationship. Inspection or test can show that a supplied assembly meets an acceptance condition. Neither should be labeled complete merely because the other exists.

For an unresolved item, record its consequence, owner and closure condition. A gap in service access may block installation; missing fault-case capacity evidence may block full-load operation. Conditional progress must name the permitted activity and restriction. Keep the matrix concise enough to use in a real review, but specific enough that another engineer can reconstruct the decision without relying on the meeting participants' memory.

slides.title: Review the Route from Dock to Position
slides.transcript:
A rack that fits its final position can still fail to reach it safely. Review the complete route from the delivery bay to the installed location, using the intended loaded configuration and approved handling method. Include packaging or temporary equipment where applicable.

Measure clearances at doors, turns and overhead obstructions. Check ramps, lift capacities, floor limits and concentrated loads at wheels, feet or handling attachments. Overall mass alone doesn't answer those questions. Center of gravity, load distribution and the handling state can change the applicable evidence.

At the final position, preserve connection and service space rather than using every available clearance as occupied footprint. Route planning should be owned by the qualified site and handling teams, not inferred from a frame's nominal dimensions. Record where equipment is installed or removed during the move and what inspection follows. Document the supported route for this configuration.

For a deeper look, check out OCP Academy's Open Data Center for AI: Applying the Specification. Its facility compatibility module walks through dock levelers, moving wheel loads, doorway and turning clearances, and lift capacity, following the move from the delivery bay to the final row.

slides.title: Lab Qualification and Real Transport Are Not the Same
slides.transcript:
Transport qualification is evidence under stated conditions, not a guarantee against every journey. The twenty twenty-six transport-vibration discussion highlights why motion in multiple directions and interactions among equipment matter. A single test result should be read with its load, fixtures, input conditions and acceptance criteria.

Ask whether the tested configuration represents the proposed shipment. Changes to equipment population, restraints, accessories, support or packaging can affect applicability. Also distinguish a frame test from evidence for the complete populated rack. The frame may survive while a connection or installed assembly becomes unacceptable.

Use the Summit material to sharpen the questions, not to invent universal shipping limits. Request the applicable qualification record and the supplier's approved handling conditions. Define receiving and post-move inspections against those conditions. If the route or configuration lies outside the supported envelope, escalate before moving the rack. A successful previous shipment is useful experience, but it doesn't close a material difference in the next deployment.

slides.title: Plan Acceptance Around Observable Results
slides.transcript:
Acceptance should produce observable results tied to requirements. Agree on the configuration, operating conditions and acceptance criteria before testing. Otherwise, a successful demonstration can become a debate about what success was supposed to mean.

The plan may include identity and revision checks, physical inspection, interface verification and agreed functional or load tests. The exact procedures belong to the qualified teams and supplier documentation. This course supplies the review logic, not a substitute commissioning procedure.

Define how exceptions are handled. An accepted deviation needs a scope, technical basis, authorized owner and any operating restriction. A temporary restriction should not vanish when the rack changes hands. Preserve the final evidence matrix, accepted configuration and unresolved items in the handover record. This makes acceptance repeatable and supports later troubleshooting. It also separates readiness for a limited activity, such as an unpowered fit check, from readiness for full operation under the required workload and fault conditions.

slides.title: Supplier Review Case: Find the Missing Evidence
slides.transcript:
Return to our deployment case. Proposal A advertises a larger rack rating, but its thermal and transport evidence doesn't identify the offered configuration. Proposal B supplies revision-matched records, while the site team hasn't closed one route constraint.

Neither proposal is ready for unconditional acceptance. The headline rating doesn't repair Proposal A's evidence gaps. Proposal B may support a bounded next step, but only if the unresolved route issue doesn't affect that activity. A conditional decision must state what can proceed and what remains blocked.

Build the short decision record. Name the missing evidence, its owner and the condition that would change the result. Compare the cost and feasibility of closing those gaps rather than treating every unknown as equivalent. Pause and decide what you'd request first from each supplier and from the site team. A defensible choice may eventually favor either proposal, but it must follow the requirements and evidence, not the order of the marketing claims.

slides.title: Why the Rack Power System Changes
slides.transcript:
As rack demand increases, the power system becomes a stronger architectural constraint. At a given voltage, more power requires more current. That affects conductors and connections, but also heat, space, service access and the way a fault is contained.

A larger shelf rating addresses only one part of the path. The input arrangement must supply it, distribution must carry it within qualified conditions, and the equipment must accept it. Cooling for conversion and distribution losses remains part of the rack review. So do the conditions after a required loss.

The engineering question isn't simply how to install more power units. It's how to deliver the requested workload through the complete path, with the required resilience and permitted behavior. Establish the boundary where capacity is claimed, whether the rating is continuous or time-limited, and which environmental and redundancy conditions apply. Those distinctions prevent an impressive installed total from becoming an unsupported operating limit.

slides.title: HPR Is a System Architecture
slides.transcript:
A high-power rack, or HPR, is a system architecture rather than a single larger component. It can combine IT equipment, power shelves, distribution and energy buffering in arrangements chosen for the deployment. Some designs separate power equipment from the IT rack; others organize it within a rack-scale assembly.

Trace the proposed physical path and the responsibilities at each boundary. Horizontal and vertical busbar arrangements belong to a specific implementation. Don't assume a familiar illustration establishes the connections for a different generation or supplier combination.

The twenty twenty-six discussion of aggregated and cascaded power shelves shows why architecture matters beyond addition. Shared inputs, distribution and control can create common constraints or common failure points. More modules can improve capacity or resilience only when the surrounding system supports the intended behavior. Start the review with the complete topology, then attach the ratings and fault cases. A bill of materials without that relationship map is not yet a usable power architecture.

entries.text: IT'S A HIGH-POWER EXTENSION OF A STANDARD ALREADY IN GLOBAL

slides.video_transcript: As AI and high performance computing workloads continue to scale, the power and cooling demands of modern data centers are reaching unprecedented levels. The Open Compute Project's High Power Rack, or HPR, addresses this challenge by extending the ORv3 standard to meet next -generation power requirements, without disrupting the foundational modularity that makes ORv3 so scalable. The motivation behind HPR is clear. Standard ORv3 racks typically support up to 18 to 36 kilowatts per rack. But with dense GPU and AI -accelerated deployments, operators are now pushing toward 100 kilowatts and beyond, towards the 1 megawatt rack. This doubling of power density demands more than just bigger power supplies. It requires a rack ecosystem rethink. That's where HPR comes in. It retains the same physical envelope and mechanical alignment as the base ORv3 standard, meaning you don't have to redesign your data center layout. Instead, HPR introduces enhanced features inside the rack to safely deliver higher power and manage thermal output more efficiently. The cornerstone of the ORv3 that continues with the HPR design is its adoption of 48V direct power distribution. Carried through a higher current, deeper designed busbar systems supported by a new extension to the back of the frame. This approach not only supports more powerful IT gear, but also improves energy efficiency by reducing conversion losses. New busbar extensions and grounding enhancements ensure safety and compatibility with OCP's evolving electrical architecture. But delivering more power is only half the story. The HPR solution also addresses the thermal challenge by integrating blindmate liquid cooling manifolds. These front -accessible modular cooling interfaces support cold plate loops directly within the rack, making it easier to manage heat generated by high wattage components. The design reduces reliance on traditional air cooling, helping facilities scale without exceeding environmental or HVAC limits. Importantly, HPR achieves all of this while remaining part of the broader ORv3 family. It's not a standalone solution. It's a high -power extension of a standard already in global deployment. That means facilities can gradually adopt HPR elements as their workload demands increase, without replacing their entire infrastructure. HPR was well -introduced at the OCP Global Summit in 2024, to support 92 kW or more. But since then, it's quickly evolving within the rack and power OCP projects community, through multiple iterations, with plans to now go to 1600 roofline rack power. In short, the high -power rack represents OCP's vision of an AI -ready, thermally resilient, and energy -optimized future. It allows data centers to meet rising demands without sacrificing the open, interoperable principles that ORv3 is built on.

slides.title: Trace the Physical Power Path
slides.transcript:
Trace the physical power path without skipping connections. Begin at the defined facility input, follow conversion in the shelf, then distribution and equipment power entry. For each segment, identify its current, voltage, thermal and fault requirements using the selected implementation.

Connections can become limiting even when the surrounding conductors appear adequate. Their applicable rating depends on the assembly and operating conditions, not just a connector family name. Likewise, a busbar drawing describes a defined interface; it doesn't validate every attachment or equipment population around it.

Keep the protective bonding path distinct from the operating return. The source grounding scheme controls those functions. Don't reinterpret a simplified course schematic as installation guidance. The review outcome is a traceable path in which no segment relies on an unrelated rating or an assumed bond. If the power shelf changes revision, revisit the affected input, output, management and mechanical boundaries instead of assuming the old integration evidence transfers unchanged.

bullets.text: Facility input → shelf conversion → distribution → equipment entry.
Review each connection and the applicable thermal/current limits.

slides.title: High Power Rack Technical Focus

figure.alt: High Power Rack Technical Focus
figure.caption: This walkthrough describes an earlier HPR implementation. Use the HPR V2 specification for the current shelf, PMM and protection requirements taught in this module.

slides.video_transcript: AI is driving power requirements dramatically. Led by Meta, the OCP Rack and Power Projects community developed with HPR to meet this demand. HPR features a 6 -inch deeper and 65 -kilogram heavier rack, primarily to increase busbar capacity from 18 kilowatts to 92 -kilowatts minimum, and upgraded power shelves from 3 -kilowatts to 5 .5 -kilowatts PSUs, totaling 33 -kilowatts per shelf. HPR also improved grounding and added room for an extra power shelf, allowing for 3 power and 3 BBU shelves. AC whips transitioned from 20A to 30A in North America. Today's most recent plans for HPR go up to 8 power shelves. The HPR rack's mechanical structure is simple. We bolted a welded extension to the standard ORv3 frame using existing mounting points. This extension supports the deeper busbar, providing protection and grounding. All standard accessories like security doors and rear heat exchanges can be used. The extension also supports up to 6 AC cable whips with integrated cable management. To maintain structural integrity and accommodate the added weight, HPR adds ballast masses at the front of the frame to ensure stability and pass UL qualifications. When designing the busbar, we considered going wider, but to accommodate platform concerns, we went deeper instead, adding 125mm for a total depth of 190mm. This increased the busbar weight from 15kg to 80kg, necessitating more robust mounting features. Instead of two screws, we now use eight at the bottom and a bracket at the top, for four mounting points. Through simulations and thermal testing in 2024, the first iteration of HPR achieved 155kW from the rack, even though real -world applications might yield slightly less. To support the higher power, we upgraded to 30A AC whips for North America, while EU maintains the 32A IEC 309 standard with two plugs instead of one. Moving from ORV3 to ORV3 HPR also shifted the rack grounding point to the busbar side, connecting the 50V return and busbar cage with metal blocks. This allows us to remove IT gear input connector ground contacts. We also changed the busbar cage material to low -conductivity steels to increase contact resistance and mitigate potential ground current. The HPR power shelf, still 1U, now outputs 33kW with 5 .5kW PSUs. We upgraded busbar output connectors to 700A and designed dedicated thermistors to monitor busbar clip temperature. HPR PSUs significantly increased peak power capability, supporting 136 % rated power for 50ms and 160 % for 400 microseconds, crucial for GPU workloads. Finally, Bennett, together with its OCP community partners, developed an Active Power Monitoring Module, PMM, with an MCU for automatic address allocation and critical parameter consolidation. All our PSU, BBU, PMM, and AC Whips specs are available on the OCP Rack and Power Wiki, with the overall rack spec coming soon.

slides.title: Nameplate Capacity Is Not Usable Capacity
slides.transcript:
Use a bounded example. Six twelve-kilowatt units give seventy-two kilowatts of installed nameplate capacity. If the required case has one unit unavailable, five units remain, giving sixty kilowatts of supply capacity before other constraints.

Now add a downstream path qualified for fifty-five kilowatts under the stated conditions. That path is tighter than the remaining supply total, so the example supports at most fifty-five kilowatts at that boundary, before any additional operating or reserve margin. Seventy-two, sixty and fifty-five answer three different questions.

The animation applies these constraints in sequence. It doesn't imply that one failed unit is equivalent to losing any possible input feed. For a real design, the required loss might remove a shared path or impose another limit. Recalculate the actual topology under that case. Usable capacity is the supported result after the relevant constraints are applied, not a nameplate sum with a redundancy label attached.

slides.title: Review Current Shelf Examples Without Universalizing Ratings
slides.transcript:
The HPR version two seventy-two-kilowatt shelf provides a current component example. Its cited options use six twelve-kilowatt power supply unit slots and state sixty kilowatts with N plus one and dual cords. The document also defines the input arrangement and a fifty volt output.

Keep those statements together. They do not mean every high-power rack delivers sixty kilowatts, or that every dual-cord failure leaves the same capacity. Review the exact option, connection and operating conditions. N plus one describes spare unit capacity relative to a requirement; it doesn't automatically provide independent redundancy across every shared part of the system.

Component specifications for the power monitoring module and connectors support this integration. They help establish the relevant interfaces, but we won't turn this rack course into a register or pinout survey. The practical task is to verify that the configured shelf, distribution and equipment combination supports the required workload and fault behavior using consistent document revisions.

slides.title: Shelves, Buffers and Fault Domains
slides.transcript:
A changing workload asks a different question from a nameplate calculation. The power path must support demand over time, including permitted transitions and the response of conversion, storage and control. Two workloads with the same average can impose different excursions.

The animation shows demand changing against a constrained delivery path. The curve is illustrative, not measured hardware performance. A buffer can supply or absorb energy within its limits, but its available energy, power and state must support the event. It doesn't create unlimited sustained supply.

Next, identify fault domains: parts of the system whose shared dependency can fail together. Multiple shelves can still share an input, bus, protection element or control dependency. Review which functions remain local and which depend on coordination. The useful outcome is a topology and response review tied to the required events, not an assumption that adding shelves or storage automatically removes every bottleneck. Specialist energy-storage material is linked for qualification depth beyond the rack boundary.

slides.title: What Power Management Owns
slides.transcript:
The power monitoring module, or PMM, provides an interface for observing and managing parts of the shelf system. Its precise functions follow the selected specification and implementation. At rack level, the important questions are what is measured, which decisions are coordinated, and what happens when communication or a controller is unavailable.

Telemetry can reveal a limit or fault condition, but observation is not the same as protection. Fast local protective behavior must not depend on an assumed software response unless the qualified design explicitly establishes that architecture. Likewise, a management command doesn't prove that every downstream device follows the intended sequence.

Record response ownership at each timescale and boundary. Ask how load sharing, capacity limits and recovery requests interact with local protection. Review degraded communication and stale or missing measurements as part of the design, not only the nominal dashboard. The PMM specification is a supporting resource here; the course's focus remains the rack-level consequence of control and visibility, not its register details.

slides.title: Lose a Supply Path, Then Recalculate the Budget
slides.transcript:
Start a fault review by naming the loss precisely. One supply unit, one input feed, one shared distribution segment and one control function can produce very different outcomes. The redundancy label alone doesn't identify which equipment remains available.

Draw the surviving path and apply its supported ratings. Then include thermal conditions and any operating restriction that follows the event. If the remaining capacity is below the requested workload, the design needs a defined response rather than an assumption that it will continue unchanged.

Recovery is another operating case. Restoring a source can introduce transitions, sharing changes or other conditions that the system must manage. Define what evidence permits restoration and who authorizes it through the approved operating process. Don't infer a live-service procedure from this conceptual review. The result should identify what the workload may do during the fault and after recovery, with a traceable technical basis for both.

slides.title: Grounding, Temperature and Service Access Remain Constraints
slides.transcript:
Capacity doesn't override the rest of the design. The protective bonding and return scheme still follows the cited implementation. Thermal conditions still determine whether the applicable component and assembly ratings are supported. Service access still has to accommodate the approved isolation and replacement method.

A high-current connection may be inaccessible after neighboring equipment and hoses are installed. A cooling change may alter the conditions under which a distribution assembly was qualified. A revised shelf can change both management and physical interfaces. These are integration changes, not paperwork details.

Review the complete populated rack and the allowed maintenance state with the qualified teams. Record the operating limits and any required restrictions. The course doesn't authorize energized work or establish safe access distances. Its purpose is to make sure those responsibilities and approved conditions are represented in the deployment decision, rather than omitted because the power calculation appeared to pass.

slides.title: Capacity Case: Can the Rack Sustain the Workload?
slides.transcript:
Our case requests fifty-eight kilowatts after one supply unit is unavailable. The remaining units provide sixty kilowatts, but the downstream path is qualified for fifty-five under the stated conditions. The requested case is not supported.

slides.title: Higher Voltage Changes Current, Not the Whole Problem
slides.transcript:
For an ideal direct-current segment, power equals voltage times current. At one hundred kilowatts, fifty volts corresponds to two thousand amperes. At eight hundred volts, the same power corresponds to one hundred twenty-five amperes. This comparison ignores losses and describes only the segment at the stated voltage.

The animation holds power constant while changing the illustrated voltage and current. It then reveals the obligations that don't disappear: insulation and connection design, protection, conversion, cooling and service arrangements. Don't convert the current ratio into a universal cable-size or efficiency claim. Actual assemblies have additional requirements and operating conditions.

Most importantly, a higher-voltage supply feeding conversion near the rack doesn't reduce current in an unchanged fifty-volt segment after that conversion. Mark the boundary before using the equation. The comparison is useful because it identifies where current burden can change. It isn't a complete architecture decision or permission to treat higher-voltage equipment as equivalent to the existing low-voltage system.

slides.title: AI Workloads Change with Time
slides.transcript:
Rack-average power hides time behavior. A workload can have the same average demand as another while producing different excursions, repetition and correlation across equipment. Those differences can matter at the rack and at the facility interface.

The twenty twenty-six power-oscillation discussion connects changing training demand to supply-side concerns. Use that context to ask what events the proposed system must support. Identify the magnitude, duration and repetition of the relevant demand changes, and the boundary where behavior is measured.

Don't infer a hardware response time or permitted excursion from a generic curve. Obtain the supported envelope and test evidence for the actual configuration. Also assign responsibility: which response is local to the equipment or rack, and which depends on the facility? A dashboard average can be useful operational information while remaining insufficient for dynamic qualification. This is why a steady-state power budget and a time-domain review complement each other rather than compete.

slides.title: Buffers, Power Sharing and Load Smoothing Serve Different Needs
slides.transcript:
Energy buffering, power sharing and load smoothing are related but different functions. A buffer stores energy and can supply or absorb power within its permitted state and operating limits. The amount of energy and the duration of an event matter as well as the peak power.

Power sharing redistributes demand or capacity within an architecture. It doesn't create unlimited supply beyond the available system. Load smoothing changes the demand presented at a selected boundary, but the workload and storage still have to obey their own constraints.

For a proposed solution, name the event and the boundary it addresses. A short buffer response may help with an excursion but cannot support an indefinitely larger sustained load. The relevant battery or capacitor system also requires its own qualification and operating controls. We link the specialist storage course rather than treating a storage icon as proof of safety or availability. At rack level, verify that the function solves the stated problem and that the complete response has evidence.

slides.title: The AI Data Center 1 Megawatt Rack: ORv3’s Future

figure.alt: The AI Data Center 1 Megawatt Rack: ORv3’s Future
figure.caption: Explore the path toward megawatt-class racks. Distinguish proposed architectures from qualified deployment limits.

slides.video_transcript: As data centers race to meet the exponential growth of AI workloads in AI factories powered in high megawatts and even gigawatts, electrical demands per rack are surging to levels once considered unthinkable to power much denser compute infrastructure. The industry is now preparing for a new benchmark, the one megawatt rack. ORv3 plays a central role in this transition. It provides a standardized foundation that can be extended to meet the needs of one megawatt rack deployments. The key is to retain the mechanical and interface consistency of ORv3 while allowing flexible enhancements that increase power and thermal capabilities without forcing a complete redesign. From a power perspective, the journey to one megawatt involves a few critical shifts. First, power must be delivered at higher voltages and through larger conductors, often in the form of overhead busways instead of traditional floor PDUs. These busways connect to high -capacity rectifiers, which then distribute power down through the racks via new high -current busbar extensions. At the rack level, internal distribution must be robust enough to handle up to 100 kilowatts or more per zone. Power shelves must support greater density and redundancy and racks must allow multiple feeds to deliver the necessary amperage safely. Throughout this architecture, grounding becomes a critical design point with careful attention paid to bonding paths, fault protection, and compliance with global safety standards. Microsoft, Meta, and Google have come together at the OCP to contribute a new way to distribute power, and thus enable the one megawatt IT rack by introducing a power rack. Instead of data center electrical busways feeding power shelves directly to the IT rack, taking up precious space that cannot be used for IT servers, this new approach implements a sidecar power rack. The sidecar rack is also based on ORV3 and high -voltage DC. This specification is named Mount Diablo, and it provides for options at 800 volts monopole DC or plus minus 400 volts, reusing the supply chain components from the electric vehicle industry. It receives the power from the facility power distribution, and then feeds it to the IT rack. Either directly to the bus bar pre -converted to 48 volts with a busbar clip connector, or an intermediate converter can be placed in the IT rack, which then feeds the bus bar at the lower voltage needed for servers. There is additional cable distribution and connector innovation required associated with the Diablo rack for safety and efficiency. But scaling power alone isn't enough, a one megawatt rack generates extreme heat. That's why liquid cooling, already part of ORV3's vision, is now a must. Cold plate loops, rear door heat exchangers, and facility water integration are all being designed as native features, not add -ons. Blindmate manifolds and front -access cooling interfaces make serviceability and safety manageable even at scale. Importantly, ORV3's open and modular architecture enables vendors and operators to adopt these innovations incrementally. A facility might start with 30 -kilowatt racks and gradually evolve toward 100 -kilowatt or more, while staying within the same rack standard. This allows for global interoperability, faster innovation, and shared learning across the OCP community. The one megawatt rack is no longer a concept, it's a necessity. ORV3 ensures that as we scale toward this future, we do so with standardization, safety, and sustainability in mind.

slides.transcript:
Open Rack Wide, or ORW, expands the mechanical envelope for different equipment packaging and rack-scale integration needs. That creates opportunities, but also changes the questions asked of the site and the complete assembly.

More width can affect internal arrangements, cable and hose routes, and service access. A larger or more integrated payload changes handling and structural considerations. None of those choices automatically establishes the electrical or thermal capacity of the installed system.

Read the ORW base specification as a shared interface contract. Then identify the implementation that supplies external dimensions, payload and other design choices. This distinction is particularly important when a proposal mixes a base-specification name with a photograph and a rating from a different configuration. Keep the source and scope attached to each claim. The review should establish why the selected arrangement suits the deployment, not simply that wider equipment can be placed inside a wider frame.

slides.title: The Evolution of Open Rack: From ORv3 to ORW

figure.alt: The Evolution of Open Rack: From ORv3 to ORW
figure.caption: Explore the wider mechanical envelope. Use ORW Base v1.0.1 and the selected implementation for exact interfaces and ratings.

slides.video_transcript: For years, the ORW base has been the undisputed foundation of efficient data center infrastructure. But the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence has fundamentally changed the physical requirements of computing. Next generation AI workloads demand massive scale up networks and larger silicon footprints. Engineers need the physical space to distribute multiple GPUs evenly across the compute tray. This balanced distribution prevents severe thermal hotspots and optimizes complex network routing. Within the boundaries of a traditional 600 millimeter wide rack, these physical layouts become a severe bottleneck. The community needed a new standard. Enter the open rack wide or ORW. This new specification literally doubles the width of the standard rack to 1200 millimeters or in inches expanding from 21 to 42. This expansion allows engineers to build massive interconnected AI platforms without compromising on modularity, but this shift is about much more than just physical space. The transition to ORW is a necessary evolution toward high power racks. This wider format provides the crucial volume required to route complex liquid cooling manifolds, seamlessly integrate high power racks, shared baseline power shelves, and support the extreme payload weight of fully populated AI clusters. By anticipating the physical demands of next generation silicon, the Open Compute project ensures that scalability and efficiency remain available to everyone. Let's take a look inside the new frame.

slides.transcript:
The extra frame volume can fill quickly when equipment, network connections, power paths and cooling lines are integrated. Routing is a shared spatial problem, not a final cosmetic step. Reserve the required envelopes before filling the remaining space.

Then review service movement: which item moves, which connections remain, and whether adjacent equipment can stay within its permitted state. A route that works at rest can become unacceptable during removal.

Include containment and residual airflow where required. A hose or cable rearrangement can affect both service access and cooling. Record the accepted arrangement and who approves changes after deployment. This prevents a later addition from quietly occupying the clearance that the original integration review relied on. slides.transcript:
The ORW base includes shared busbar geometry and electrical requirements for IT equipment. Use those interfaces to connect the frame review to the actual power path, while retaining implementation-specific capacity and operating conditions.

The animation reveals the rack boundaries and a short requirement-level power-entry sequence. The equipment's power-entry control prevents powering before the input connector is fully asserted and turns it off before removal, as described in the specification. It doesn't invent contact timing, an internal precharge circuit or a live-service procedure.

Cooling needs its own evidence. Identify the manifolds, couplings, equipment interfaces and receiving loop in the selected implementation. A shared mechanical frame doesn't guarantee common fluid conditions or thermal performance. Attach the electrical and thermal records to the same configured system used in the payload review. This is how the wider frame becomes an integrated rack decision rather than a mechanical approval with unexamined subsystems added afterward.

slides.transcript:
Our case has supporting evidence for the proposed frame and equipment arrangement. The route review, however, has not established acceptance for one constrained loaded-move segment. Structural evidence doesn't close that site issue.

Assign the route issue to the responsible site and handling teams, with a clear closure condition. If they change the handling configuration or remove equipment for the move, revisit the affected evidence and post-move verification. Pause and identify the exact record that would permit the decision to change. The goal is not to accumulate paperwork, but to ensure the requested activity is supported by the configuration, route and operating conditions that will actually occur.

slides.title: Follow Heat Through the Complete Rack Loop
slides.transcript:
Follow heat beyond the coupling. Equipment transfers heat to coolant, the rack routes it through its manifold and connections, and the receiving system must carry it to an adequate heat-rejection path. A coolant distribution unit, or CDU, may separate the technology cooling system from the facility water system.

The technology cooling system, often called TCS, serves the equipment side of that boundary. The facility water system, or FWS, serves the receiving side in the illustrated arrangement. These terms locate responsibilities; they do not imply identical fluid chemistry or operating conditions on both sides.

Keep the residual air-side heat visible. A liquid path that meets its own requirement can coexist with insufficient airflow for other components. The system review needs both. Define where temperatures, flows and pressures are guaranteed, and which party demonstrates heat rejection under the agreed operating cases. The linked CDU course provides specialist depth without replacing the configured-rack acceptance evidence.

slides.video_transcript: We have built the structural frame and we have delivered the power. Now we must cool the system. With the open rack wide supporting extreme density AI clusters, advanced liquid cooling is a mandatory requirement. To manage the immense weight of the IT gear within the expanded 1200 millimeter width, ORW utilizes a unique mechanical substructure known as the canister. This heavily reinforced chassis ensures rigid support and precise alignment as the massive server nodes slide into the rack. This mechanical precision is absolutely critical. To extract the massive heat load. Thick vertical cooling manifolds are mounted securely into the expanded side channels of the ORW frame. Keeping the fluid completely separate from the central power delivery. Connecting a multi 100 pound server into these vertical manifolds requires absolute perfection. The solution is the pivoting blind mate coupling or PBMC. As the canister slides into the rack, the PBMC system automatically aligns the fluid connectors. It utilizes a brilliant mechanical pivot to absorb the extreme weight and positional tolerance of the hardware, ensuring a zero leak fluid lock without any manual intervention. The engineering behind this connection is a masterpiece of open hardware design. Let's take a closer look at exactly how the PBMC mechanism engages in our next interactive deep dive.

slides.transcript:
A cooling connection is an operating interface, not just a pair of matching fittings. Verify the exact fluid specification and the wetted materials, including seals, tubing, couplings and equipment. A generic coolant family name isn't sufficient evidence of compatibility across the assembled loop.

Match required and available conditions at the defined boundary. Temperature, flow and pressure requirements interact with the configured circuit and workload. Review permitted transients and degraded conditions as well as the normal operating point. Don't assume a component's maximum rating is the system's intended operating condition.

Record who provides each condition and how acceptance establishes it. If the receiving loop's commitment is unresolved, the rack-side component ratings cannot fill the gap. The dedicated cooling-fluids Academy course supports a deeper material and chemistry review. Our rack-level task is to ensure that the selected components and receiving systems share a supported operating envelope, with no hidden assumption about compatibility or responsibility.

The manifold distributes coolant through a defined arrangement. The coupling must work within the relationship those assemblies create.

Review alignment and deflection across the complete tolerance chain, not only at an isolated connection. Then include the space needed for installation and service. A support arrangement can be structurally acceptable while placing a connection outside its permitted mating condition.

The source-derived plate shows the relevant parts without inventing an internal mechanism. Use the controlling drawings and supplier requirements when geometry matters. Check that cable and hose routing doesn't impose unintended loads or obstruct movement. The resulting review should establish that the configured equipment can be supported, connected and serviced under its qualified conditions, rather than assuming a common assembly name guarantees every interface around it.

slides.title: PBMC: Align, Engage and Establish the Fluid Path
slides.transcript:
The Pivoting Blind Mate Coupling, or PBMC, defines plug and socket interfaces for a blind-mate fluid connection. The specification describes pivoting behavior that supports the permitted alignment relationship. It is not inherently limited to one rack frame.

The animation uses the source drawings and staged highlights. It identifies the plug and socket, the pivoting compliance and the defined mate-distance relationship. It does not invent internal sealing stages, an audible click or a universal self-centering mechanism. The specification leaves relevant internal design choices to suppliers while establishing interface and performance requirements.

Evaluate the selected coupling against its permitted mate distances, misalignment, forces, fluid conditions and qualification. A blind-mate label doesn't promise perfect alignment, zero leakage under every condition or unrestricted live replacement. Those claims require scoped evidence and approved system procedures. The correct mental model is a specified interface operating within demonstrated limits, integrated into a supported mechanical and hydraulic system.

slides.title: Flow, Pressure Drop and Residual Air Heat
slides.transcript:
Flow depends on the hydraulic system, not a single component rating. Hydraulic impedance describes how a path resists flow. Equipment, couplings, hoses and manifolds contribute to the configured path, and parallel branches can receive different flows under the same overall system conditions.

Don't use a pump's headline rating or a coupling size as proof that each equipment branch receives what it needs. Establish the available conditions at the required boundary and verify the circuit under the supported equipment population. Changes to routing or components can change that result.

Keep pressure limits and heat rejection in the same review without treating them as interchangeable. Adequate flow doesn't by itself establish an acceptable receiving temperature, and a thermal rating doesn't prove mechanical pressure compatibility. Residual air-side heat still needs its own supported path. The linked thermal-boundaries course gives deeper context; here, retain the complete path and the evidence at each handoff.

slides.title: Identify a Fault, Contain It and Restore Service
slides.transcript:
A cooling fault needs a defined response, not a promise that a coupling cannot leak. Detection may come from pressure, flow, temperature or other qualified monitoring. The meaning of a signal and the required action depend on the configured system and approved operating process.

The animation separates detection, containment and recovery. It is a conceptual response map, not a valve-operating or live-maintenance procedure. Identify which equipment is affected, which protective functions act locally, and who owns the decision to isolate or reduce load.

An alarm clearing doesn't necessarily establish that the cause is resolved or that full operation is supported. Verify the required restoration conditions, inspect or test as the approved procedure requires, and obtain the appropriate authorization before returning to service. Preserve the event and configuration record. This prevents a nominally healthy display from standing in for evidence that the affected mechanical, fluid, electrical and thermal interfaces are ready again.

slides.title: Prepare Commissioning and Handover Evidence
slides.transcript:
Commissioning and handover connect design intent to an accepted operating system. Preserve the installed configuration and document revisions, the conditions tested, the acceptance results and any restrictions. Include the limits the operator must maintain at electrical and thermal handoffs.

Identify monitoring and response ownership. The operator needs to know which signals matter, which actions are automatic, and which require an authorized procedure or another team. An exception accepted during deployment must remain visible after the project team leaves.

Also define change triggers. Replacing equipment, changing fluid, rerouting hoses or updating a control revision can affect previously accepted interfaces. Not every change requires the same review, but none should be assumed harmless solely because the rack still powers on. A concise, traceable handover record supports operation, recovery and later integration. It is part of readiness, not an administrative step after readiness has already been declared.

slides.transcript:
Consider a rack that fits its supports and has adequate electrical capacity, but cannot sustain the requested workload because the receiving loop doesn't meet the required thermal conditions. The mechanical and power checks can remain valid while the operating case fails.

Trace the heat path to locate the actual boundary mismatch. Don't immediately blame the coupling or install a larger power shelf. A change to flow, temperature, heat rejection or the equipment envelope must be supported by the responsible design and site teams.

The review decision is to hold the unsupported operating case. A reduced or bounded activity may be possible only with its own justified conditions and restrictions. Record what evidence would close the thermal gap. The linked Project Brazos material offers relevant context for cooling integration in an existing facility, but it doesn't replace this site's commitments. A rack is a system of interfaces precisely because a pass in one domain cannot compensate for a blocking gap in another.

slides.title: Sustain the Deployment Through Change
slides.transcript:
The evidence record remains useful after commissioning. Equipment generations change, suppliers revise components, and operators adjust workload or cooling conditions. Preserve enough configuration and revision control to recognize when the accepted envelope has changed.

Review the interfaces affected by a proposed change. A new component may fit while changing current demand, heat rejection, alignment or control behavior. A fluid change can affect multiple wetted materials. A revised handling arrangement can change which loaded-route evidence applies.

Shared interfaces create opportunities for reuse and replacement, but substitutions still need a supported basis. Scale the review to the consequence of the change and retain the decision and restrictions. This is how openness becomes a practical operational benefit: more qualified options with traceable boundaries, rather than more combinations whose behavior is assumed. The same method supports future rack architectures even when their dimensions, voltage or equipment packaging differ from today's examples.

slides.video_transcript: The open rack wide is no longer just a design specification. The OCP ecosystem is actively building and deploying this massive infrastructure to power the next generation of artificial intelligence. Today, we are looking at how the industry brings this architecture to life. To accelerate adoption, engineering teams develop internal reference solutions to prove the architecture at scale. A prime example is the AMD Helios AI rack, which is built on foundational OCP designs originally contributed. By Meta and Ridal, Helios serves as a highly optimized reference instantiation of the ORW specification. By looking at the Helios compute trays, you can see the true value of the 1200 millimeter width. The design showcases how larger AI accelerators, closely and efficiently packed scale-up networking, expansive memory configuration, and liquid cooling manifolds all integrate seamlessly with a single continuous chassis. But the open hardware ecosystem thrives on adaptation. Partners take these reference designs and deliver fully realized turnkey commercial solutions. For example, the HPE co-branded Helios deployment combines 72 AMD instinct GPUs with purpose-built Ethernet scale-out networking and advanced direct liquid cooling. And with new ORW implementations from partners like Super Micro being announced, the market for ORW infrastructure is expanding rapidly. From reference designs to massive commercial deployments, the Open Rack Wide is actively reshaping the modern data center. But AI is moving fast, and next, we will explore the extreme megawatt trends pushing this hardware to its absolute limits.

questions.prompt: Which items belong in controlled recovery and handover after a cooling fault? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Verify the fault condition is contained and the authorized restoration conditions are met.
Record the accepted configuration, operating limits, monitoring and response owners.
Reassess affected interfaces after relevant equipment, fluid or revision changes.
Restore load solely because an alarm has cleared, without checking the cause or operating envelope.

questions.feedback_correct: Recovery needs verified conditions and authorized action. Handover preserves configuration, limits, responsibilities and change control; an alarm clearing alone is not proof.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Select verified restoration conditions, documented handover and revalidation after relevant changes. Do not restore load based only on a cleared alarm.
